subject: Biology
title: Enzymes: Biological Catalysts
description: A quick, practical guide to Enzymes: Biological Catalysts.

hook.text: Chemical reactions in your body would take years without help. Enzymes finish them in milliseconds.

buildup.text: Each enzyme has a specific shape that fits one molecule—like a lock and key.

discovery.text: Enzymes lower the activation energy for reactions without being used up themselves.

twist.text: A single enzyme can process thousands of reactions per second without wearing out.

climax.text: Too hot or too acidic and enzymes unfold, losing their shape and function forever.

punchline.text: Life's speed depends on molecular matchmakers.

quiz.question: How do enzymes speed up reactions?

details.summary: Enzymes are protein catalysts that dramatically speed up chemical reactions in cells without being consumed. They work by lowering activation energy and are highly specific, with each enzyme fitting its substrate like a lock and key or through induced fit.
details.whyItMatters: Without enzymes, most cellular reactions would take years. They enable life-compatible speeds for thousands of simultaneous reactions. Enzyme deficiencies cause metabolic diseases, and enzyme inhibitors are the basis for many drugs.
takeaways: Enzymes lower activation energy to speed reactions by millions of times
Each enzyme is specific to particular substrates based on shape
Temperature and pH affect enzyme shape and therefore function

faq.question: How do enzymes speed up reactions so dramatically?
faq.answer: Enzymes bind substrates in their active site, orienting them optimally and straining bonds to lower the activation energy needed for the reaction. Some enzymes accelerate reactions by a factor of a trillion or more compared to the uncatalyzed rate.

faq.question: Why do fevers affect enzyme function?
faq.answer: Enzymes work best within narrow temperature ranges. Moderate fever speeds reactions slightly, which helps fight infection. But high fever denatures enzyme proteins by disrupting their shape, which is why sustained high temperatures are dangerous.
